title: RT-DETRv3: Real-time End-to-End Object Detection with Hierarchical Dense Positive Supervision

problem.summary: RT-DETR's one-to-one Hungarian matching provides much sparser supervision than the one-to-many assignment of dense detectors like the YOLO series, leaving both encoder and decoder under-trained and the model short of its optimal accuracy.
statements: Hungarian one-to-one matching yields sparse supervision that causes insufficient training of encoder and decoder.
Dense-supervision CNN detectors (YOLO series) train more fully under one-to-many label assignment while keeping a speed/accuracy trade-off.
Standard DETR's high computational complexity limits its practical application, so real-time variants must keep its lightweight framework.

evidence.quote: However, compared to dense supervision detectors like the YOLO series, the Hungarian matching provides much sparser supervision, leading to insufficient model training and difficult to achieve optimal results.

However, the Hungarian matching strategy provides sparse supervision during training, leading to insufficient training of both the encoder and decoder, which limits the optimal performance of the approach.
However, its high computational complexity significantly limits its practical applications.

background.summary: The method builds on RT-DETR/RT-DETRv2 (real-time end-to-end DETR with hybrid encoder and IoU-aware query selection) and on auxiliary one-to-many training strategies from Co-DETR, DAC-DETR, MS-DETR and Group DETR; the gap claimed is that those dense-supervision works are not real-time detectors.

relatedWork.name: RT-DETR
relatedWork.relation: framework that RT-DETRv3 keeps and extends
relatedWork.quote: RT-DETR [32] is the first real-time end-to-end transformer-based object detection algorithm.

relatedWork.name: RT-DETRv2
relatedWork.quote: RT-DETRv2 [19] further enhances the flexibility and practicality of RT-DETR [32] by optimizing the training strategy to improve performance without sacrificing speed, although requires longer training time.

relatedWork.name: Co-DETR
relatedWork.relation: prior one-to-many auxiliary head training strategy
relatedWork.quote: Co-DETR [33] proposed multiple parallel one-to-many label assignment auxiliary head training strategies (e.g., ATSS [30] and Faster RCNN [20]), which can easily enhance the learning ability of the encoder in end-to-end detectors.

relatedWork.name: YOLO series
relatedWork.quote: The current CNN-based real-time object detectors are mainly the YOLO series.

evidence.quote: DAC-DETR [9], MSDETR [31], and GroupDETR [4] mainly accelerate the convergence of the model by adding one-to-many supervised information to the decoder of the model.
However, due to their one-to-one sparse supervision, the convergence speed and final effect are limited.

solution.summary: RT-DETRv3 keeps RT-DETR's architecture and adds three training-only hierarchical dense positive supervision branches: a CNN one-to-many auxiliary head (PP-YOLOE) on encoder features, multi-group mask self-attention perturbation that diversifies positive query assignment across query groups, and a shared-weight one-to-many decoder matching branch.
solution.approach: Densify positive supervision for both encoder and decoder with one-to-many auxiliary branches and perturbed multi-group self-attention, all discarded at inference so latency is unchanged.
components: CNN-based one-to-many auxiliary branch using the PP-YOLOE head on encoder features C3/C4/C5
ATSS matching early in training switched to TaskAlign matching
mask generator producing random perturbation masks for multiple query sets
mask self-attention module perturbing attention weights of each query group
shared-weight one-to-many decoder branch matching each ground truth with 4 queries
total loss L = alpha*L_aux + beta*L_o2o + gamma*L_o2m with all weights 1

evidence.quote: we introduce a CNN-based auxiliary branch that provides dense supervision that collaborates with the original decoder to enhance the encoder’s feature representation.
This strategy diversifies label assignment for positive samples across multiple query groups, thereby enriching positive supervisions.
Notably, all aforementioned modules are training-only.

To alleviate the problem of sparse supervision in encoder output caused by the decoder’s one-to-one set matching scheme, we introduce an auxiliary detection head with one-to-many assignment, such as PP-YOLOE [28].

experiments.summary: RT-DETRv3 (R18/R34/R50/R101) is evaluated on COCO val2017 against the RT-DETR series and CNN real-time detectors in AP, latency and convergence, with ablations on each supervision branch and on the number of perturbation branches; latency is measured on a T4 GPU with TensorRT FP16.

evidence.quote: RT-DETRv3-R18 achieves 48.1% AP (+1.6%/+1.4%) compared to RT-DETR-R18/RT-DETRv2-R18, while maintaining the same latency.
RT-DETRv3-R101 can attain an impressive 54.6% AP outperforming YOLOv10-X.
our approach maintains the same inference speed as both RT-DETR [32] and RT-DETRv2 [19].

limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that the framework is not yet optimized for lightweight deployment and that larger RT-DETRv3 models tend to overfit COCO; strong results also rely on long 72/120-epoch schedules.
items: The overall framework has not been optimized for lightweight deployment, leaving inference efficiency on the table.
As model size grows, RT-DETRv3 tends to overfit, attributed to a mismatch between dataset size and model size.
Long training schedules are used: 72 epochs for R50/R101 and 120 epochs for R18/R34.

evidence.quote: As illustrated in Figure 4, we noticed that as the model size increases, RT-DETRv3 tends to exhibit overfitting.
We used a 10x (120 epochs) training schedule for smaller backbones (R18, R34) and a 6x (72 epochs) training schedule for larger backbones (R50, R101).

futureDirections.direction: Optimize the whole RT-DETRv3 detector framework for lightweight deployment to further improve inference efficiency.
futureDirections.quote: However, since we have not yet optimized the overall framework of the RT-DETRv3 detector for lightweight deployment, there is still room for further improving the inference efficiency of RT-DETRv3.

futureDirections.direction: Counter overfitting of larger models with additional training data such as Objects365.
futureDirections.quote: when we added additional training data, the performance of RT-DETRv3 continues to improve as the training epochs increase, and it performs better than the model without the additional data at the same epochs.

applications.domain: autonomous driving, video surveillance, object tracking
applications.detail: Real-time detection is said to have enormous practical value in these applications, and the field demands inference speeds above 30 FPS.
applications.quote: It has enormous value in practical applications such as autonomous driving, video surveillance, and object tracking.

applications.detail: Real-time detection is framed as having higher requirements on algorithm performance, such as inference speed greater than 30 FPS.
applications.quote: Real-time object detection has higher requirements for algorithm performance, such as inference speed greater than 30 FPS.

deploymentClaims: All added supervision modules are training-only and are discarded during evaluation, so inference latency is unchanged.
Latencies of all models are tested on a T4 GPU with TensorRT FP16, following RT-DETR.
RT-DETRv3 needs only 72 epochs to reach superior accuracy versus detectors training for 300-500 epochs.

evidence.quote: Since these modules are only involved during the training phase, they don’t affect the inference latency of RT-DETR [32].
Moreover, the latencies of all models are tested on T4 GPU with TensorRT FP16, following [32].
We have observed that, in comparison to most detectors employing longer training epochs, RT-DETRv3 only needs 72 epochs to achieve superior accuracy.
